title: Steady-state GPU starvation detection and graceful queue triage
creator: Ava Martinez
description: Follow-up ticket for the hosted-API GPU exhaustion incidents in Jan–Feb 2025. The incident pattern: long-running steady-state load that slowly increased KV cache pressure and queue depth, leading to token-level throttling and a delayed autoscaler response. This ticket captures the detection signal design, a triage playbook for graceful request handling during slow-capacity loss, and engineering tasks to reduce amplification from tenant prefetch and cold-KV churn. Aim: prevent repeat customer-visible throttling while preserving throughput and avoiding overprovisioning.
incident_timeline: 2025-01-29: First customer report of elevated 503s and elevated generation tail latencies in eu-west-1 hosted pools.
2025-01-30: Automated alert - GPU pool queue depth exceeded soft threshold for 12h; autoscaler triggered but failed to reclaim capacity due to nested AZ imbalance.
2025-02-02: On-call rotated, temporary mitigation applied: tenant admission caps and prefetched request backoff (soft limit).
2025-02-07: Post-incident review flagged persistent KV-cache churn and sustained small-batch traffic from a handful of large tenants as contributing factors.
2025-02-10: Raw telemetry and flamegraphs collected; hypothesis recorded: steady-state starvation + delayed autoscale hysteresis + KV pollution => queue buildup and tenant thrashing.
root_cause: Several interacting issues: (1) KV cache eviction patterns caused by high diversity in prompt prefixes for heavy tenants, causing sustained GPU memory pressure; (2) autoscaler hysteresis tuned for burst events (fast increase) not for slow steady-state increases, so scale-up lagged; (3) no early-warning signal that correlated per-tenant KV miss rate with queue growth; and (4) admission control was binary and reactive rather than progressive, causing large sudden sheds when thresholds were crossed.
mitigation_playbook: Short-term: implement progressive tenant pacing and soft admission steps; add a KV-miss-rate early-warning metric and alert; temporarily pin suspect tenant traffic into a low-priority lane during recovery windows. Medium-term: adjust autoscaler to include KV-memory pressure and slow-trend signals; implement adaptive admission that degrades model variants or reduces max sequence length for affected tenants. Long-term: cache-aware placement and tenant-coalescing to reduce cross-tenant eviction amplification.
action_items: (A1) Add KV-miss-rate and per-tenant cached-state-pressure metric to telemetry and dashboard — owner: Priya Desai — due: 2025-03-05
(A2) Implement progressive admission controller with 3 soft-shed levels (deprioritize, limit-seq-len, reject) and a PID-based ramp rather than hard cut — owner: Ravi Shah — due: 2025-03-20
(A3) Autoscaler change: include long-window slope (30m) of queue depth and KV-memory pressure as inputs; reduce hysteresis for slow-trend scale-up — owner: Miguel Alvarez — due: 2025-03-17
(A4) Run synthetic replay tests with tenant-mix that reproduces KV churn and measure amplification factor; create bench PR and dashboard — owner: Sasha Kim — due: 2025-03-12
(A5) Update runbook: add early-warning thresholds, tenant soft-isolation steps, and communication templates for customers — owner: Lily O'Connor — due: 2025-03-10
(A6) Customer follow-up: contact top-10 heavy tenants in EU region with mitigation options and optional limited sandbox to test sequences — owner: Maya Chen (SRE) — due: 2025-03-15
(A7) Explore model-variant fallback: fast-quantized variant that reduces token compute for degraded mode — owner: Research (cc: Ethan Park) — due: 2025-04-01

notes: Telemetry observation: KV miss correlation with queue depth had a stronger signal than raw GPU memory utilization for these incidents.
Risk: progressive admission may affect latency-sensitive SLAs. We will gate it behind tenant-level opt-out and test on low-latency tiers first.
Decision: prefer soft-degrade (sequence length cap, quantized fallback) over full rejection where possible to avoid customer-visible errors.
Experiment: plan an A/B test where 10% of traffic uses adaptive admission vs control to measure true customer impact on p95 latency and error rates.
